quests.instruction: Paint a clear, concrete picture in one sentence. Fit the three key words into your answer naturally.
quests.prompt: A friend is thinking of renting near you. Describe your street with two adjectives.
quests.sampleAnswer: My street is quiet and clean, so it's easy to sleep at night.
quests.hint: Put both adjectives after 'is' and join them with 'and'. Add what the result is for a person.
quests.explanation: Two adjectives after 'is' give a quick, balanced description, and 'so' links the description to what it means in real life.

quests.instruction: Write a description in one sentence that a stranger could picture. Include the three key words.
quests.prompt: Tell a friend what you thought of the last film or video you watched.
quests.sampleAnswer: The film was funny, but the ending was a little sad.
quests.hint: Describe the whole thing first, then give a different opinion about one part.
quests.explanation: Describing a whole and then a part ('the film... the ending...') shows more than a single opinion can.

quests.instruction: Paint a clear, concrete picture in one clear sentence. Work in each of the three words.
quests.prompt: A hotel asks for feedback about your room. Give one good point and one bad point.
quests.sampleAnswer: The room was comfortable, but it was a bit noisy at night.
quests.hint: 'A bit' makes a complaint softer. Add when the problem happened.
quests.explanation: Softeners like 'a bit' and 'a little' make criticism sound polite, and 'at night' makes it specific.

quests.instruction: Write a natural reply in a single sentence. Your answer should contain all three key words.
quests.prompt: Your housemate is making a chore chart. Say which job you always do.
quests.sampleAnswer: I always wash the dishes after dinner.
quests.hint: Put 'always' before the main verb, then name the job and when you do it.
quests.explanation: Adverbs of frequency come before the main verb: 'I always wash', not 'I wash always'.

quests.instruction: Answer in a single sentence, adding one useful detail. Make sure all three words fit the meaning.
quests.prompt: A doctor asks how often you exercise. Answer honestly.
quests.sampleAnswer: I sometimes walk to work, maybe two or three times a week.
quests.hint: Use 'sometimes', then add a rough number so the doctor can understand how often.
quests.explanation: A frequency word alone is vague. Adding 'two or three times a week' gives the exact information a doctor needs.

quests.instruction: Compare the two options in a single sentence. Your answer should contain all three key words.
quests.prompt: Someone asks if you are ever late. Compare work or class with social events.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm never late for work, but I'm usually late for parties.
quests.hint: Use two frequency words with 'but' to contrast two situations.
quests.explanation: Two frequency adverbs joined by 'but' let you give an honest, balanced answer in one sentence.

quests.instruction: Respond in one sentence in a way that suits the situation. Include the three key words.
quests.prompt: A customer asks when your shop or office is open. Give the days and hours.
quests.sampleAnswer: We are open from nine until five, Monday to Friday.
quests.hint: Give the hours with 'from ... until', then the days.
quests.explanation: 'From ... until' marks the start and end of a period, which is exactly the information a customer needs.

quests.instruction: Write a natural reply in a single sentence. Fit the three key words into your answer naturally.
quests.prompt: A classmate missed the announcement. Tell her when the English class starts this week.
quests.sampleAnswer: The class starts on Thursday at half past six.
quests.hint: Use 'on' with the day and 'at' with the time.
quests.explanation: Time prepositions follow fixed rules: on + day, at + clock time, in + month or season.

quests.instruction: Give a recommendation in one sentence and say why. Work in each of the three words.
quests.prompt: A tourist asks when the best time to visit your area is.
quests.sampleAnswer: The best time to visit is in April, when the weather is mild and the streets are less crowded.
quests.hint: Give a month or season with 'in', then add a 'when' clause to explain why.
quests.explanation: A 'when' clause turns a bare fact into a reason the visitor can trust.

quests.instruction: Answer the question directly in one sentence. Use all three words naturally.
quests.prompt: Say one thing you find easy and one thing you find hard in your job or studies.
quests.sampleAnswer: Reading is easy for me, but writing long emails is difficult.
quests.hint: Use 'but' between the two opposite ideas.
quests.explanation: 'But' joins two ideas that go in opposite directions, so your answer shows both sides in one sentence.

quests.instruction: Reply as you would in a real conversation in one clear sentence. Your answer should contain all three key words.
quests.prompt: A friend asks what you need to do this evening. Give two tasks in order.
quests.sampleAnswer: I need to call the bank and then buy some milk.
quests.hint: Put the tasks in the order you will do them and use 'then' for the second.
quests.explanation: 'And then' shows sequence, so the listener knows which task comes first.

quests.instruction: Write a natural reply in one sentence. Use all three words naturally.
quests.prompt: A friend asks about a restaurant you tried. Give one good point and one bad point.
quests.sampleAnswer: The pasta was good, but the restaurant was very expensive.
quests.hint: Start with the positive point, then use 'but' for the problem.
quests.explanation: Putting the positive first and the negative after 'but' gives a fair review that sounds balanced.

quests.instruction: Give your reason in a single sentence. Work in each of the three words.
quests.prompt: Your teacher asks why you are late. Give a short, honest reason.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm sorry I was late because the traffic was terrible.
quests.hint: Apologize briefly and give the reason after 'because'.
quests.explanation: A short apology plus a specific reason is more polite than a reason alone.

quests.instruction: Give your reason in one clear sentence. Each word should appear in your answer.
quests.prompt: A friend asks why you are smiling.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm smiling because I got good news this morning.
quests.hint: Reuse the verb from the question, then add 'because' and the cause.
quests.explanation: Repeating the question's verb ('smiling') makes your answer clearly connected to what was asked.

quests.instruction: Give your reason in one clear sentence. Use all three words naturally.
quests.prompt: Someone asks why you choose to walk instead of taking a bus.
quests.sampleAnswer: I walk to work because it's free and it wakes me up.
quests.hint: Give two short reasons after one 'because', joined by 'and'.
quests.explanation: One 'because' can introduce two reasons if you join them with 'and'.

quests.instruction: Paint a clear, concrete picture in a single sentence. Include the three key words.
quests.prompt: You are on a video call. Tell your colleague what you are doing right now.
quests.sampleAnswer: Right now I'm sitting at my desk and reading the meeting notes.
quests.hint: Use 'am' plus -ing for both actions, and start with 'Right now'.
quests.explanation: The present continuous describes actions in progress at the moment of speaking, so it pairs naturally with 'right now'.

quests.instruction: Paint a clear, concrete picture in one sentence. Your answer should contain all three key words.
quests.prompt: Look out of the nearest window. Tell a friend what people are doing.
quests.sampleAnswer: Outside, some people are walking to the station, and a few are waiting for the bus.
quests.hint: Use 'are' plus -ing for a group of people. 'Some ... and a few ...' separates the groups.
quests.explanation: 'Some' and 'a few' let you describe different groups doing different things in one sentence.

quests.instruction: Write a natural reply in a single sentence. Each word should appear in your answer.
quests.prompt: Your friend calls and asks where you are. Say where you are and what you are doing.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm on the platform, waiting for the train.
quests.hint: Say your position first, then add what you are doing.
quests.explanation: Place first, action second is the natural order when someone asks 'Where are you?'

quests.instruction: Say how the two things differ in one clear sentence. Include all three key words.
quests.prompt: Compare two ways of traveling in your area.
quests.sampleAnswer: The bus is cheaper than the train, but the train is faster.
quests.hint: Use 'than' after the first comparison and 'but' to show the trade-off.
quests.explanation: A comparison with a trade-off ('cheaper... but faster') is more informative than saying one option is simply better.

quests.instruction: Compare the two options in one clear sentence. Work in each of the three words.
quests.prompt: Compare your current home with a place you lived in before.
quests.sampleAnswer: My new place is bigger than my old one, but it's farther from the center.
quests.hint: Name both places and give one advantage and one disadvantage.
quests.explanation: Short adjectives take -er (bigger), and 'than' connects the two things being compared.

quests.instruction: Say how the two things differ in one sentence. Each word should appear in your answer.
quests.prompt: You are choosing between two jackets. Say which is better value.
quests.sampleAnswer: The blue jacket is more expensive than the grey one, but it looks better.
quests.hint: Long adjectives use 'more' (more expensive). 'Better' is irregular.
quests.explanation: 'Good' becomes 'better', not 'gooder', and long adjectives use 'more' instead of -er.

quests.instruction: Write the message in a single sentence in a polite tone. Fit the three key words into your answer naturally.
quests.prompt: Your hotel room has no towels. Ask the front desk politely.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hello, could you send two towels to room 204, please?
quests.hint: Start with 'could you' and add the item and the room.
quests.explanation: 'Could you...?' is more polite than 'Give me...' and is standard in service situations.

quests.instruction: Describe the plan in a single sentence. Use the three words meaningfully.
quests.prompt: Tell a friend one skill you want to learn this year.
quests.sampleAnswer: I want to learn how to swim before the end of the year.
quests.hint: Use 'want to' plus a base verb, then add a time limit.
quests.explanation: Adding a time frame ('before the end of the year') turns a wish into a goal.

quests.instruction: Give your reason in a single sentence. Make sure all three words fit the meaning.
quests.prompt: You are unwell. Explain to your manager why you have to stay home.
quests.sampleAnswer: I have to stay home today because the doctor said I need rest.
quests.hint: 'Have to' expresses an obligation. Give the outside reason with 'because'.
quests.explanation: 'Have to' shows that something is required by a situation, not just wanted.

quests.instruction: Answer the question directly in a single sentence. Your answer should contain all three key words.
quests.prompt: A visitor asks who to talk to about a lost room key.
quests.sampleAnswer: You can ask the person at the reception desk downstairs.
quests.hint: Answer with a role, not a name, and add where to find that person.
quests.explanation: Answering 'who?' with a role and a location is more useful than a name the visitor does not know.

quests.instruction: Answer the question directly in one clear sentence. Fit the three key words into your answer naturally.
quests.prompt: Someone asks when the last train leaves on weekdays.
quests.sampleAnswer: The last train leaves around eleven thirty, so don't be late.
quests.hint: Give the time first, then a short helpful warning.
quests.explanation: 'Around' makes a time approximate. A short extra warning shows you understand why the person asked.

quests.instruction: Explain in one clear sentence so the reason is easy to follow. Work in each of the three words.
quests.prompt: A friend asks why the library is closed today. The sign says 'Repairs'.
quests.sampleAnswer: It's closed today because they're doing repairs.
quests.hint: Use the information on the sign to build your 'because' clause.
quests.explanation: Reporting information from a sign or message in your own words is a real-life skill.

quests.instruction: Reply as you would in a real conversation in one clear sentence. Your answer should contain all three key words.
quests.prompt: The teacher asks each student to say something about themselves. Include a habit and a contrast.
quests.sampleAnswer: I study at night, but on weekends I usually go running.
quests.hint: Use 'but' to contrast two parts of your week.
quests.explanation: Combining a frequency word with 'but' lets you describe two different routines in one sentence.

quests.instruction: Tell what happened in one clear sentence, in the right order. Each word should appear in your answer.
quests.prompt: Say how you found this class or course and why you chose it.
quests.sampleAnswer: I found this course online because a friend recommended it.
quests.hint: Use a past verb for what you did, then 'because' for the reason.
quests.explanation: This answer mixes past tense (found, recommended) with a reason clause, a pattern that appears in most personal stories.

quests.instruction: Say what will happen in a single sentence. Include the three key words.
quests.prompt: Say what you will do to practice English every week and why.
quests.sampleAnswer: I will write a few sentences every day because it makes me more confident.
quests.hint: Use 'will' for the commitment and 'because' for the motivation.
quests.explanation: A plan is stronger when it has a frequency ('every day') and a reason.
